item.title: Application Security through Iron Man's mind
item.description: A free e-book that uses the evolution of Tony Stark's armor to explain practical Application Security.
item.content:encoded:
Software security, version after version

Tony Stark did not build a perfect suit of armor on his first attempt. He worked with the resources available, survived the immediate problem, learned from failure and created a better version.

That evolution is a useful way to explain Application Security.

Application Security through Iron Man's mind is a free e-book that connects situations from the Marvel Cinematic Universe to practical secure development. The objective is not to turn fiction into a framework, but to use a familiar reference to make security decisions easier to visualize.

The central idea

Secure software does not arrive fully formed. It evolves through requirements, hypotheses, tests, incidents, corrections and new engineering cycles.

Tony Stark's first armor was not created to defeat every possible threat. It needed to address the context of the cave, the resources available and the immediate objective of escaping.

The same reasoning appears throughout the book: security must consider threats, objectives, context and capacity. A control that is perfect for another system may be insufficient or unnecessary for yours.

What the book covers

Threat Modeling

The book uses the creation of the Mark I and the Hulkbuster to show how threats, objectives and security requirements can be considered before execution.

The discussion includes essential questions:

  • What can go wrong?
  • Which impact must be avoided?
  • Which mitigations are possible with the resources available?
  • Does the control reduce the threat that actually matters?
  • What did previous incidents teach us?

DevSecOps

The DevSecOps section organizes the transformation around four pillars:

  • culture and people's participation;
  • process and strategy;
  • tools for scale;
  • automation as an operational capability.

The message is direct: adding a scanner to a pipeline does not create collaboration or guarantee that findings will be fixed.

Vulnerability Management

Finding vulnerabilities is only the beginning. The book discusses process, tools and the need to address problems in an organized way, with priority, responsibility and learning.

Application Monitoring

An application cannot be protected if nobody understands its normal behavior. Logs, information and observability appear as essential elements for identifying anomalies and responding more effectively.

Application Security Program

The final chapters connect individual practices to an AppSec program. The focus moves from isolated activities to a continuous capability inside the software development lifecycle.

Who it is for

The book was written for anyone involved in software development:

  • developers;
  • QA professionals;
  • DevOps and SRE;
  • architects;
  • security professionals;
  • technical leaders and Security Champions.

You do not need to be a Marvel specialist. The book explains the context used by each analogy, although it contains spoilers from the movies.

Done is better than perfect, as long as it evolves

The Mark I was enough for a specific scenario. Remaining on the Mark I forever would have been irresponsible.

Software works in the same way. A first version may accept known limitations, but the team must record risk, learn from real use and evolve. Security stops being a final approval and becomes part of every new version of the armor.

The English e-book is available as a direct download.

item.title: AppSec, Motherfucker: a manifesto against security theater
item.description: Why AppSec must move beyond compliance theater and return to honest conversations about decisions, engineering and real risk.
item.content:encoded:
AppSec needs to start telling the truth again

Many organizations say they practice Application Security because they run a scanner, receive a penetration test report or have an approval step in the pipeline.

That does not mean the software is safer.

AppSec, Motherfucker is a manifesto against security treated as process decoration. It exists to provoke those who have turned secure development into a checklist, dashboard or compliance ritual with no practical consequence.

The problem is not a lack of tools

Tools are necessary. SAST, DAST, SCA and other technologies help find problems at a scale manual analysis could never reach.

The mistake begins when the tool's output becomes the objective.

A scanner can produce thousands of findings while the organization still does not know:

  • which applications carry the most risk;
  • who should fix each problem;
  • which findings matter in the current context;
  • what should actually block a delivery;
  • whether a corrected vulnerability is gone from production.

A tool is a sensor. AppSec is the system of decisions, responsibilities and actions built around that sensor.

Compliance is not the destination

Compliance can establish a baseline, require evidence and make responsibilities visible. Passing an audit, however, does not guarantee that the right technical decisions are being made.

Real security appears in design, code, pipelines, operations and incident response. It must work under deadline pressure, around legacy systems and when a finding does not have an obvious answer.

The manifesto questions the distance between the documented process and the process that actually runs.

Who the manifesto is for

This is for:

  • AppSec professionals tired of producing reports nobody uses;
  • developers who receive findings without context;
  • managers who confuse alert volume with risk reduction;
  • teams that added scanners to a pipeline and called it DevSecOps;
  • organizations that want a more honest security conversation.

It is not a maturity framework or a ready-made implementation methodology. It is an invitation to stop operating on autopilot and examine what current practices actually deliver.

How to use the provocation

Read it, disagree with it and bring the questions to your team.

Observe the pipeline that runs, not only the diagram. Choose one important finding and follow its complete path to remediation. Verify who decides, who receives context, how long it takes and how the solution is validated.

If the process cannot answer those questions, another tool will probably not solve the problem.

The name is intentionally uncomfortable. Security theater should be uncomfortable too.

item.title: Codes & Consequences
item.description: A strategic AppSec training game where product, security, budget and reputation decisions produce consequences.
item.content:encoded:
AppSec is learned by making decisions

Traditional training can explain concepts. The problem is that real work rarely presents a question with four options and only one correct answer.

In practice, teams must balance delivery, security, budget, deadlines, reputation and risk. Every choice solves one problem and may create another. Codes & Consequences turns that tension into a learning experience.

It is a strategic Application Security training game that simulates development cycles inspired by agile methods. Participants make decisions as a technology team and must deliver a functional system without losing control of security.

How the experience works

During each cycle, the team decides where to invest its resources. New features compete with fixes, controls and security activities. Vulnerabilities, incidents, unexpected events and cyber threats change the situation throughout the journey.

The game does not reward the team that simply chooses security in every round. It requires balance.

Participants need to consider:

  • business value and functionality;
  • technical risk and vulnerabilities;
  • budget and team capacity;
  • product reputation;
  • consequences created by previous decisions.

The objective is to reach the end with a product that works, preserves resources and maintains an acceptable level of risk.

Why use a game

A decision that people experience is easier to remember than a rule shown on a slide. When a harmless-looking choice creates an incident two rounds later, the relationship between cause and consequence stops being abstract.

The activity helps teams discuss topics such as:

  • security debt;
  • vulnerability prioritization;
  • trade-offs between speed and protection;
  • communication between development, product and security;
  • the accumulated impact of small decisions;
  • shared responsibility across the SDLC.

Learning happens in the conversation between participants. No tool makes the decision on behalf of the team.

Who it was created for

Codes & Consequences works as an activity for developers, AppSec professionals, DevOps, Security Champions, Product Owners, technical leaders and other people involved in software development.

It can also be used in:

  • corporate training;
  • secure development workshops;
  • Security Champions programs;
  • conferences and events;
  • technical community meetings;
  • activities that connect security and engineering.

What remains after the game

The game creates a shared language. After the experience, terms such as risk, debt, incident, priority and consequence no longer belong exclusively to the security team.

More importantly, participants see that security is not a separate step at the end of the process. It is part of the choices that build the product during every cycle.

Codes & Consequences does not teach AppSec through memorization. It puts decisions on the table and lets the consequences do the rest.

item.title: DevSecOps Podcast
item.description: Real conversations about AppSec, DevSecOps and technical decisions that must survive production.
item.content:encoded:
DevSecOps is not a checklist

The DevSecOps Podcast was created to discuss software security as it happens in the field: with context, disagreement, limitations and decisions that must continue to work after the code reaches production.

A tool is not a strategy. A scanner is not an AppSec program. Compliance does not replace engineering. These principles guide the podcast's conversations.

About the show

The podcast explores Application Security and DevSecOps through technical discussions, interviews, professional experience and analysis of real cases.

Episodes are useful to both newcomers and experienced professionals. The objective is not to oversimplify every problem, but to make each subject accessible without removing the complexity that matters.

Recurring topics include:

  • secure development culture;
  • Security Champions;
  • SAST, DAST and vulnerability management;
  • threat modeling;
  • CI/CD and automation;
  • Product Security;
  • cloud and Zero Trust;
  • AppSec careers and education;
  • artificial intelligence applied to security.

Production is the truth

One of the show's central ideas is that controls must survive the real environment. A process can look excellent in a presentation and still fail when it meets deadlines, legacy systems, false positives, dependencies between teams and delivery pressure.

The conversations therefore focus on operational questions:

  • Who is responsible for making the decision?
  • What can a developer fix with the available evidence?
  • When should a task be automated, and when does it require human review?
  • How can risk be reduced without turning the pipeline into a permanent blocker?
  • Does the control work in production, or only in the document?

People and perspectives

The show is hosted by Cássio B. Pereira and includes security, development and market professionals. Marcos Santos and Ben-Hur Santos are part of the podcast team, alongside guests who bring experience from different companies and specialties.

That diversity matters because AppSec does not happen inside a single role. Software security depends on collaboration between the people who design, build, operate, test, prioritize and take responsibility for products.

How to follow

The official website brings together episodes, search, tags and related material. The show is also available as video and through different podcast applications.

RSS remains the most direct option for following the show without an algorithm.

  • Open the official website ↗ (abre em nova aba)
  • Browse the episodes ↗ (abre em nova aba)
  • Follow the podcast channels ↗ (abre em nova aba)

The DevSecOps Podcast exists to turn security into a conversation engineering teams can use. No checklist as the final destination. No tool taking the place of strategy.
